paragraphs: November 15, 1990: Cupertino wins a design patent for the Apple Extended Keyboard II, arguably the greatest computer keyboard of all time.

Delivering the perfect combination of durability, feel and a pleasing click-clack sound, the Extended Keyboard II will become a mainstay of pro-grade Apple setups during the early 1990s — and perhaps the best-loved keyboard in Apple history. Courtesy of an ADB-to-USB adapter, some people continue to use these input devices today.
In an era when Apple typically obsesses over making everything thinner, lighter and more minimalist, the Extended Keyboard II stands as a glorious reminder that sometimes bigger really is better.

This hulking mechanical keyboard delivered something today’s sleek accessories often sacrifice: a deeply satisfying typing experience. Its spring-loaded Alps switches, crisp click-clack sound and thoughtful ergonomic touches made it a cult favorite that some Mac users still refuse to give up.

The original Extended Keyboard arrived in 1987, after Steve Jobs left Apple following his battle with CEO John Sculley. In the same way that Macs of that era focused on extendability in a way Jobs never approved of, the Apple Extended Keyboard models — of which the Extended Keyboard II is the best — included function and arrow keys Jobs did not like.

The Apple co-founder likely would have appreciated the quality of the keyboard, however. It combined high-end components with the kind of clever proprietary touches that make Apple products great. For instance, it used mechanical key switches made by Japan’s Alps Electric Co., which later produced keyboards for the iMac.

The keys felt ridiculously responsive. The sound left no doubt about whether you had hit a key. And the keys snapped back at an impressive speed after you pressed them, thanks to physical springs under each keycap.

The Apple Extended Keyboard II included a couple of other neat touches, too. Its Caps Lock key remained depressed when you hit it (unlike today’s keyboards, which usually indicate they are on by way of an LED). This gave the keyboard a typewriter-style feel that many users appreciated. The keyboard also boasted a power switch, which drew many accolades in the early 1990s.
